title: Research Journal #37 — How We Checked the Gravity of a Straight Particle Beam
html:
Before Bending the Beam, We Needed to Check the Straight One

One of the challenges in researching unfamiliar physics is knowing whether a computer calculation is telling us something meaningful.

A computational verification may produce numbers that look reasonable. It may even run without errors. But neither of those things establishes that the mathematics has been implemented correctly.

On September 19, 2026, Beyond the Light Barrier reached an important milestone in its wormhole communication (WC) research. We completed a controlled computational verification of the predicted gravitational response of idealized relativistic matter, including a steady straight particle beam.

The experiment was designated WC-PO-1.7C-V1.

It did not demonstrate faster-than-light communication. It did not detect gravity from a particle accelerator. What it established was narrower, but important: within a defined mathematical model and parameter range, our numerical implementation reproduced the expected analytic results and passed its specified verification checks.

That gave us a stronger computational foundation for investigating more complicated beam configurations.

Why Start With a Straight Beam?

Our earlier research had led us to investigate relativistic particle beams as possible sources of extremely small, controlled gravitational effects.

According to general relativity, matter and energy contribute to spacetime curvature. A moving particle beam therefore has a gravitational contribution, although the predicted effect is extraordinarily small.

The challenge is not simply to calculate a number. We need to know whether the calculation correctly represents the chosen physical model.

A straight beam provides a useful starting point because simplified versions of its gravitational response can be calculated analytically. Those expressions give us reference values against which to test a numerical implementation.

This is a standard scientific strategy: begin with a case where the expected answer can be calculated directly, verify the method within that case, and only then investigate more complicated situations.

For our research, the central question became:

Could our software recover the predicted transverse gravitational acceleration and velocity impulse from idealized relativistic matter, while preserving the assumptions and limitations of the calculation?

Freezing the Experiment Before Running It

On September 19, 2026, at 19:58:18 UTC, we froze the scientific specification for WC-PO-1.7C-V1 before beginning implementation.

That specification identified the equations, physical assumptions, supported parameter ranges, numerical methods, acceptance thresholds, and required negative tests.

The distinction matters.

If we were free to change the acceptance criteria after seeing the results, we could unintentionally make an unsuccessful calculation appear successful. By freezing the design first, we established a documented standard against which the subsequent results could be judged.

The experiment used linearized general relativity: an approximation that treats the gravitational disturbance as small relative to flat spacetime.

It considered two distinct idealized sources:

  • A steady, infinitely long straight beam, used to calculate transverse gravitational acceleration.
  • A moving point-like packet of matter, used to calculate the small change in a test particle's transverse velocity as the packet passes.

These are separate mathematical source models. The point-packet calculation is not a measurement of the steady beam.

Neither source represents a complete accelerator with magnets, support structures, electromagnetic fields, finite beam dimensions, and all associated energy and stresses.

What Gravity Did the Mathematics Predict?

For the steady beam, the analytic model predicted an inward transverse gravitational acceleration:

a⊥ = 2GP(1 + β2) / (βc3ρ).

Here, G is Newton's gravitational constant, P is the total beam energy crossing a fixed plane per second, c is the speed of light, β is the source speed divided by c, and ρ is the transverse distance from the beam.

The expression predicts that the gravitational acceleration decreases as the distance from the idealized beam increases.

For the separate moving point-packet model, the first-order transverse velocity impulse was:

Δv⊥ = 2GE(1 + β2) / (βc3b),

where E is the packet's total laboratory-frame energy and b is its transverse impact parameter.

A velocity impulse is a change in velocity accumulated during the passage of the source. It is not the same thing as a sustained acceleration.

Both expressions depend on the source's speed. Massive particles cannot travel at exactly the speed of light, so our calculations needed to retain the finite-speed correction rather than treating the ultrarelativistic limit as exact.

The analytic expressions were derived for the experiment's prescribed stress-energy sources within linearized general relativity. The software then calculated gravitational responses through its implemented tensor and field operations, rather than simply returning the benchmark expressions.

This distinction was essential to the internal verification, although both the benchmark and implementation were developed within the same project.

What the Verification Found

For the steady-beam reference case, the specification used a source speed of 99.9999% of the speed of light, a transverse distance of one centimeter, and an idealized total beam energy flux of one trillion watts.

The resulting transverse gravitational acceleration was approximately:

9.91 × 10⁻²² meters per second squared.

That is an extraordinarily small acceleration.

For the separate moving point-packet case, using a total energy of one million joules and a one-centimeter impact parameter, the predicted velocity impulse was approximately:

9.91 × 10⁻²⁸ meters per second.

These are computational predictions within idealized mathematical models, not measured physical effects. The specified beam energy flux is not an assertion that a practical accelerator could deliver or sustain such a source.

The specified finite-speed analytic comparisons passed the frozen relative-error threshold of 10−12. This tolerance evaluated numerical agreement with the chosen equations; it was not an estimate of the physical accuracy of the idealized source model.

The internal verification also examined source-energy scaling, distance scaling, particle-speed corrections, exact zero-source results, and rejection of inconsistent or unsupported inputs.

The archived analytic and scaling verification matrix reported 78 passing checks out of 78.

The broader software regression suite reported 713 passing tests, including 44 new tests associated with this experiment.

These results support the conclusion that the implementation reproduced the specified analytic behavior within the tested domain.

They do not constitute independent scientific reproduction or establish that the idealized source fully describes a real accelerator.

An Important Lesson About Numerical Accuracy

One of the most instructive findings came from the moving point-packet calculation.

The software evaluated the gravitational velocity impulse numerically over a finite interval. As the numerical resolution increased, the calculated value approached the analytic answer for that same finite interval.

The observed convergence was approximately fourth order, consistent with the selected composite Simpson integration method for this smooth integrand.

That was a successful numerical verification.

But there was another question: did the finite integration interval include the entire idealized gravitational interaction?

It did not.

The omitted portion of the infinite-time analytic integral accounted for approximately 0.7722% of the full impulse.

That was much larger than the remaining numerical quadrature error.

In other words, the numerical method accurately calculated the selected interval while still excluding a known portion of the complete idealized interaction.

We preserved that distinction explicitly rather than presenting the finite-window result as the full-time impulse.

It illustrates why numerical convergence alone is not enough. A calculation can converge correctly and still answer a narrower question than a reader might assume.

From Local Verification to an Approved Research Milestone

The experiment preserved its frozen specification, implementation, regression tests, numerical results, convergence evidence, and limitations.

The final archived run was designated run-003. Earlier runs were retained as distinct records of the experiment's development and reporting.

The final archive contained 725 immutable objects, and its recorded integrity verification passed.

Following review, the experiment received an explicit owner-approved PASS disposition and was committed to the BTLB-SIM GitHub repository on September 19, 2026, at 7:28 p.m. Central Daylight Time.

The approved experiment commit was:

73872af84b119c3c5cfdb73094f2eff255894f2c

The committed record preserves the original pre-commit review as well as the subsequent approval. The earlier pending status is therefore part of the historical record, not a contradiction of the later PASS disposition.

This milestone is classified as Category 7 — computational verification under the Beyond the Light Barrier Research Method. The analytic benchmarks are Category 6 calculations.

It was not independently reproduced or physically demonstrated.

What We Had Not Established

Several important questions remained open.

The model did not include the complete stress-energy accounting of a real accelerator. It did not establish whether the predicted gravitational effect could be separated from electromagnetic interference, vibration, environmental gravitational variations, or instrument noise.

It did not demonstrate that a practical detector could measure the effect.

The idealized infinitely long beam is not a globally realistic accelerator configuration. The point-like packet introduces a mathematical singularity that is excluded from the evaluated exterior field. The calculation also uses a prescribed source and a leading-order test-particle trajectory rather than solving the full nonlinear Einstein equations.

Nor did the experiment establish any faster-than-light communication mechanism.

These limitations were not incidental qualifications added after the result. They were part of the declared scientific scope.

The result increased confidence in the correctness of the implementation for the specified mathematical problem. It did not reduce the unknown physical uncertainties associated with building a real source or detecting its gravitational signal.

What This Milestone Made Possible

The straight-beam and point-packet tests provided internally verified implementations of specific analytic predictions, within the frozen model and parameter envelope.

That matters when moving toward more complicated source configurations.

If a later calculation involving a bent beam produces an unexpected result, we need to distinguish behavior introduced by the new geometry from an error already present in the underlying implementation.

The verification constrained one potential source of error: the implementation of these particular analytic gravitational responses. It did not eliminate new assumptions, numerical challenges, or physical constraints introduced by a curved beam.

That is how we want Beyond the Light Barrier to progress: not by treating every successful calculation as evidence of a breakthrough, but by establishing what each result actually supports before relying on it in the next investigation.

The milestone was not that we had discovered a way to communicate faster than light. It was that we had verified, within bounded computational tests, that our implementation recovered the gravitational response predicted by the models we were using.

That is a smaller claim—and a scientifically useful one.

  1. Braun et al., arXiv:2504.10942v1 (2025), theoretical steady-beam gravitational benchmark. https://arxiv.org/html/2504.10942v1

  3. Tiesinga et al., CODATA Recommended Values of the Fundamental Physical Constants: 2018, Reviews of Modern Physics 93, 025010 (2021). https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.93.025010
